title: Idalia Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Idalia wells have a 300-foot median depth; local drilling estimates run $16,500-$28,500 for a finished well.
h1: What Idalia Wells Are Like Before You Buy or Build
intro_html:
For rural property around Idalia, the local well records point to a relatively consistent depth range but incomplete production information. Within five miles, Colorado DWR records include 421 permitted wells, with 206 recorded as constructed. A total of 253 report depth, 75 report pump yield, and only 12 report static water level.

That means the area data is useful for planning, but it cannot guarantee what a new well will do on one specific lot. The best comparison is a group of nearby wells, followed by a site-specific review of permits, aquifers, septic layout, and the proposed building location.

sections.heading: Idalia well depth: plan around the middle of the local range
sections.html:
Reported wells near Idalia have a median depth of 300 feet. The middle half runs from 249 to 310 feet, so a driller bidding a typical site should be working in that neighborhood rather than assuming a shallow plains well. The deepest recorded well is 500 feet.

Depths are split between the 100-to-300-foot range, which accounts for 47% of records, and the 300-to-600-foot range, which accounts for 51%. Only 2% are under 100 feet, and none are recorded above 600 feet. The local geology is described in the cost model as alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. Nearby Vernon, Kirk, Joes, Wray, Burlington, and Laird can provide additional comparison points, but the closest wells still matter most.

sections.heading: What an Idalia well may produce
sections.html:
The reported yield numbers are generally encouraging, but the sample is limited to 75 wells. The median pump yield is 20.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 15.0 and 50.0 gallons per minute. Records show 76% producing more than 15 gallons per minute.

Another 21% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 3% are between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. No recorded wells are under 1 gallon per minute. These figures describe tested or reported wells, not a promise for an unbuilt well. Ask for the actual well test, production method, and intended household or irrigation use. A domestic well also remains subject to its permit conditions, including applicable exempt-well limits.

sections.heading: Water levels around Idalia and what the records show
sections.html:
Only 12 wells report a static water level, so this part of the local picture is much thinner than the depth data. Among those records, the median depth to water is 204 feet, with the middle half from 178 to 230 feet.

That gives a useful planning point for pump setting, casing, and electrical work, but it is not enough to establish a long-term water-table trend. The permit history spans the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit issued in 2024, yet the supplied water-level records are not reported as a decade-by-decade series. Do not assume the water table is either stable or falling without checking nearby measurements and the well construction report.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Idalia, and how recent is the history
sections.html:
Idalia’s permit history is spread across several decades. The records show 9 permits from the 1950s, 12 from the 1960s, 46 from the 1970s, 30 from the 1980s, 32 from the 1990s, 44 from the 2000s, 16 from the 2010s, and 14 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2024.

The most active names in the records are Schaal Drilling Co. (Schaal, Ruben T.) with 48 wells, Wellstone Industries Dba Twiss & Wilson Drilling Inc (Twiss, Raymond L.) with 29, and Parrish Drilling (Parrish, Wayne) with 17. This is permit history, not a recommendation or proof of current availability. Confirm licensing, insurance, scheduling, casing and grout specifications, testing, and the exact scope of a written bid.

sections.heading: Idalia well drilling cost: a practical budget
sections.html:
For the local ground conditions of alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the 300-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $10,500-$16,500. This is the hole only, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $16,500-$28,500. A deeper-than-typical hole, difficult access, extra casing or grout, longer utility runs, and site conditions can move the final bid. Compare proposals line by line: planned depth, casing, grout, pump size, test requirements, trenching, electrical work, and what happens if the first target does not produce enough water.

sections.heading: Idalia risks to check before construction
sections.html:
Low yield is not the dominant result in the available records, but production data exists for only 75 wells. Dry holes and disappointing wells remain possible, especially when a buyer relies on a broad area median instead of nearby construction reports. A fractured-bedrock or unnamed aquifer is listed for 269 wells, while 139 name the Ogallala and 13 name the High Plains Aquifer. The records show no Denver Basin aquifer wells.

Water quality also needs its own investigation. There are 13 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, although no historic mine features and no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites are mapped. Test the well water before relying on it. Check septic setbacks, soil and drainage, building access, and the permitted use. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be needed for some uses; read the DWR permit rather than assuming household use covers every plan.

sections.heading: A sensible Idalia plan for buying or building
sections.html:
Before closing, pull the DWR permit and construction report for the subject property and compare it with wells nearest the lot. Confirm the permitted use, total depth, casing and grout, pump information, static water level, and any recorded test. Because only 206 of the 421 permitted wells are recorded as constructed, do not treat every mapped permit as a completed, producing well.

For a vacant lot, have the driller and septic designer review access, the well location, building envelope, septic area, and electrical route together. For an existing home, test the water, inspect the pressure system, and verify the well can serve the intended use. A Colorado DWR permit controls what the well may do. If irrigation, livestock, additional residences, or other uses are planned, get the water-rights and augmentation question answered before buying.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Idalia, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Idalia is 300 feet. The middle half runs from 249 to 310 feet. About 47% are between 100 and 300 feet, while 51% are between 300 and 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 500 feet, so a buyer should budget around the local median but review the closest construction reports.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Idalia?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $35-$55 per foot for alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 300-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $10,500-$16,500. A finished system including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $16,500-$28,500. The final bid can change with depth, access, casing, grout, and utility distance.

faq.q: How much water do Idalia wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 75 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 20.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 15.0-50.0 gallons per minute. Records show 76% above 15 gallons per minute, 21% from 5 to 15, and 3% from 1 to 5. These are reported wells, not a guarantee for a new well on a particular parcel.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Idalia?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from well depth or yield. There are 13 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles of Idalia, so test water from the property before drinking it. The area has no mapped historic mine features and no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Use a qualified laboratory and test for contaminants appropriate to the site and permit history.

faq.q: What should I check before buying land with a well near Idalia?
faq.a: Review the Colorado DWR permit, construction report, permitted use, depth, pump information, and water-level records. The area has 421 permitted wells, but only 206 are recorded as constructed, 253 report depth, 75 report yield, and 12 report static water level. Also confirm septic placement, access, electrical needs, water quality, and whether planned uses require an augmentation plan.
